b: Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), both emerging and officially designated, consist of approximately 600 schools in 31 states, DC, and Puerto Rico. They enroll over 5 million students from a wide array of racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic backgrounds, including two-thirds of all Hispanic/Latine undergraduates in the US (per data for the year 2024–25). Research released from the Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities (HACU) on Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) shows a 5% increase in the number of HSIs over a two year period from 2022–2024. Although similar to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges in terms of the student demographic, HSIs have only in recent decades become widely recognized as a key pillar in the access-oriented education model in the United States. Importantly, HSI designation has been granted to an incredibly heterogeneous pool of schools, from elite institutions such as UT Austin to community colleges.

Our discussion highlights our home institution, Kean University, New Jersey’s fourth largest state institution, an R2 Carnegie designated regional-public, access-oriented HSI that offers more than 50 undergraduate majors, 70 graduate programs (spanning doctoral, master’s, and certificates), and 14 online programs, as well as campuses across New Jersey and the Pacific at Wenzhou-Kean, China. In 2022, Kean University awarded degrees to 915 Hispanic/Latine students, which was a 30.7% share of our graduates. In Fall 2024, approximately 38% of Kean students identified as Hispanic, 21% as Black or African American, 50% were Pell Grant eligible, and 46% were first-generation college students. As of Fall, 2026, Kean University has continued to expand its HSI population through its historic merger with New Jersey City University, now Kean Jersey City. In what follows, we share the pressing questions and insights that shaped our dialogue on actionable strategies that elevate Hispanic/Latine student success while simultaneously expanding the landscape of English Studies at HSIs.

We believe there is untapped potential for the majority of our students, faculty, and staff who navigate multiple linguistic worlds, including but not limited to fluent bilinguals, heritage speakers, and those learning English or Spanish. Such innate linguistic sensitivity to nuance is ideal for the study of literary translation. Investing in translation programs at regional public HSIs similar to those found at Kent State or Boston University can prepare students for impactful, cross-sector careers in a variety of fields. Such support might come in the form of dedicated coursework, faculty training on multilingual rhetorics, community translation projects, bilingual writing workshops, and/or partnerships with local organizations and publishers.

To be clear, we are not proposing that English programs at regional public HSIs swallow programs in translation studies or Spanish. Rather, we envision translation and multilingual rhetoric scholars as key partners in helping Hispanic/Latine students succeed. Interconnected perspectives from writing studies and translation studies might offer student opportunities to produce research and creative works in multiple languages, while perspectives from a combined English and Spanish literary studies might examine how different languages and methods of storytelling shape meaning, argumentation, and communication across global spaces. Hispanic/Latine students are certainly not a monolith, and a redesigned English studies space can highlight and build upon the strengths of Hispanic/Latine cultural and linguistic diversity. A curriculum that centralizes translations of Hispanic/Latine texts would support and maintain the rich history of ancient and contemporary Hispanic/Latine cultural practices. With US college student demographic changes on the horizon, now is the time to reconceptualize the recruitment pool for the future of literary and writing study.

For HSIs, English programs with a global and translational emphasis only further prepare students for careers in translation, interpretation, international business, diplomacy, education, journalism, human rights, and technology. And this list can go on! A more globally focused English major can prepare students for any career where cross-cultural communication and linguistic expertise are needed.
1. How does our English department and university at large already contribute to our Hispanic/Latine community? What can we do better?

The English department at Kean University is a tripartite program comprising writing studies, literature studies, and the ESL department. Within writing studies and literary studies, courses like Ethnic American Literature and Writing for Social Change foster critical perspectives between culture, narrative, and power. Our World Literature course, part of our General Education curriculum for Kean students, requires a minimum of one work in translation within the course. Our ESL department works closely with Supera, the university’s Spanish speaking program, to offer general education and discipline-focused courses, academic advisement, and tutoring in Spanish. Outside of English studies, Kean also has a Latin American studies minor and a Latino Student Organization and is the home of the first Latina based sorority, Lambda Theta Alpha (established 1975). In 2025, the English department worked closely with Kean’s Common Read to host former United States Poet Laureate Juan Felipe Herrera and create multilingual curriculum and extracurricular programming based on his collection of poems Every Day We Get More Illegal.

English studies plays a pivotal role in shaping a dynamic and globally minded academic citizenry. Today, a majority of the discourse around the future of English studies has focused on historically elite and/or well-funded institutions. While we recognize the significance of analyzing and defending the role of English studies at these institutions, we note with concern that this discourse has often left out the vast majority of students who enroll in English programs at access-oriented colleges and universities around the United States. HSIs have the potential to re-energize and reconfigure English studies as a discipline that cultivates academic rigor, advances social mobility in both literary and nonliterary professions, amplifies cultural agency, and sustains campus community engagement for historically underrepresented and underserved students.

Just as HBCUs are positioned to advocate for a mosaic of Black voices, HSIs are uniquely positioned to amplify a multiplicity of Hispanic/Latine voices (of all races) in publishing and media and build pipelines for students into the literary world.
2. What type of postgraduation benefits would this nuanced curriculum offer students?

Claiming to be in the service of career prep for low-income students, university administrators around the nation continue to push for defunding a wide variety of humanities programs. For minority serving, access-oriented colleges and universities, much of the conversation on the English major focuses on the supposed wastefulness of a humanities degree. Many in higher ed forefront the incorrect assumption that English majors cannot secure jobs postgraduation. Within this conversation is the implication that the English major (and other humanities/liberal arts majors) is reserved for the economic elite; that is, for students who have the time and resources to discuss “frivolous” topics within the literary arts without concern for economic mobility.

In the face of political attacks against the arts and humanities, funding cuts at colleges and universities, and the never-ending discussion about the utility of the English major in the 21st century, highlighting the work that English graduates pursue is more important than ever. Many of us understand how the English major equips students with critical thinking, communication, and analytical skills that are highly valued across industries. Just as HBCUs are positioned to advocate for a mosaic of Black voices, HSIs are uniquely positioned to amplify a multiplicity of Hispanic/Latine voices (of all races) in publishing and media and build pipelines for students into the literary world. A cross-disciplinary curriculum that advances translation studies can also equip our already predominantly bilingual students with advanced skills and industry connections, preparing them for careers in literary, technical, legal, and humanitarian translation, in addition to roles in publishing, editing, and education.

3. We believe education is more than a means to an end. We don’t just want our students to get jobs. We want their education to transform their thinking. Beyond career preparation, how can English studies cultivate meaningful experiences for our campus community?

Establishing non- and extracurricular programming that aligns with academic objectives is the scaffolding to successful community life at every university. At Kean, numerous initiatives foster meaningful, interactive community experiences. One example is our Common Read Program, which builds connection through the shared act of reading the same book. The program distributes the community-selected book to campus members for free, hosts multilingual poetry readings, paint nights, and faculty panels.

Building on models like the Common Read, English departments at regional, access-oriented public HSIs can further cultivate belonging and expand community life on and off campus through special collections that spotlight the history and impact of Hispanic/Latine literature and art. At major research HSIs, such collections serve as permanent spaces to explore Hispanic/Latine heritage, support original scholarship, and preserve literary history. At regional public HSIs, special collections that connect with the heritage and experiences of the university community have the potential to empower the campus’s cultural and intellectual growth. A small collection dedicated to Hispanic/Latine literature produced in both English and Spanish, for example, could revitalize classroom discussions, on campus theater productions, and collaboration with neighboring libraries and museums.

For our own institution, we further wonder what this initiative would look like if we spotlighted New Jersey artists and writers of the Hispanic/Latine diaspora such as Celia Cruz, Hilda A. Hidalgo, and Judith Ortiz Cofer. Such a collection could showcase Hispanic/Latine creatives whose work is primarily in English, Spanish, and/or Spanglish, highlighting an important complexity within the US-based diaspora. Literary special collections at regional public HSIs that focus on locally rooted artists and authors would demonstrate to both the university community as well members outside the institution that their own cultural narratives are essential to the broader study of English studies and academic life. With institutional support for more localized special collections around the nation, HSIs of all kinds could continue to affirm their role in uplifting and celebrating our country’s rich multicultural literary traditions.
4. How can already overburdened educators and staff sustainably implement multilingual, equity-conscious initiatives?

Sustaining these objectives requires dedicated and strategic institutional support for students, staff, and faculty. It would further require not just the insight and expertise from faculty, but an investment at the university administrative and state funding levels. These investments would better cultivate an interdisciplinary, multilingual community of scholars and students. A conscientious approach to time management that prioritizes flexibility, accessibility, and the avoidance of overburdened schedules is essential to fostering student and employee well-being.

The reality is that most of our students at Kean work, many full-time. Committing to a no-conflict schedule (or close to it) when it comes to special events would fortify community engagement, ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to participate and support one another’s gatherings, rather than feeling overwhelmed by too many choices.

To further support our students, Kean University’s Career Services has been hard at work emphasizing the benefits of partnering with university majors to host industry-specific events. Kean’s Office of Accreditation and Assessment now shares job placement data with individual departments, recognizing that faculty can provide valuable insights for student success. By tracking employment trends like the percentage of English majors entering publishing, marketing, education, or transitioning into tech roles like UX or content writing, English departments have the opportunity to utilize faculty insight and connections to further benefit student career initiatives. Understanding common and unique career paths would also allow for faculty to refine course offerings, advising, and professional development.

For such collaborative efforts to be done with detailed integrity, we believe this work must be compensated and not treated as yet another addition to service for the university. Beyond curriculum, stronger ties with Career Services, mentorship programs with humanities alumni, and targeted recruitment events can challenge misconceptions about English degrees and open career opportunities.

With more robust institutional investments in multilingual faculty, training in multilingual rhetorics, programming centered on the Hispanic/Latine experience, and strong partnerships with Career Services, English studies at regional public HSIs can continue to focus on both passion for knowledge building that speaks truth to power and preparation for career success beyond the classroom.

We contend that English studies, when intentionally structured to reflect the multilingual and multicultural realities of today’s students, is not simply relevant. In fact, English studies is indispensable in preparing the next generation of scholars, storytellers, and global professionals.

The questions we have posed above are not abstract. They form our guiding principles for reimagining English studies at HSIs, which are uniquely positioned to redefine the value of English studies in the 21st century. At institutions like Kean University, the study of literature and writing is not, as Audre Lorde proclaimed, a luxury. Multilingualism is a form of empowerment, a method of making sense of the world, and a pathway to shape the future. In sharing our insights and strategies, we hope to contribute to a broader conversation about equity, community, and the transformative power of public humanities-centered higher education.
